Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Name Reminders: Hearing related names, Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Vignette:
Elena has come to believe that her life is now divided into two distinct eras: before the storm, and after. At fifty-seven, the first era feels like a lifetime ago, a memory belonging to a different woman. It has been two years since Hurricane Alma, and the water has long since receded, but for Elena, the flood is a constant presence. She works as a physical therapist, a profession built on helping others regain strength and stability, yet she feels as though her own foundations have been washed away.

The storm arrived with a ferocity that defied all warnings. Elena remembers the sound most vividly—a relentless, deafening roar of wind and rain that seemed to be tearing the world apart. Then came the water, first seeping under the door of the home she had lived in for thirty years, then pouring through the windows. The smell of mud, sewage, and decay filled the air, and a wave of nausea rose in her throat that has never quite left. She remembers wading through the chest-high, contaminated water, the grief hitting her with the force of a physical blow as she looked back at her submerged life.

In the months that followed, Elena found a small, second-floor apartment, believing the height would offer a sense of security. But safety remained elusive. Her world, once expansive, began to shrink until only the four walls of her apartment felt manageable. She is on constant alert, startled by the gurgle of pipes in the wall or the rumble of a garbage truck on the street below, each sound a potential harbinger of disaster. Sleep offers little respite; she lies awake for hours, listening, waiting. Going out requires a monumental effort of will that she can rarely muster. This has had tangible consequences for her work. She had to ask her supervisor to reassign all of her patients who used the clinic's hydrotherapy pool. The sight of that large, still body of water was unbearable, a placid mask for the destructive power she knew it held.

Her experience of the trauma itself has become fragmented and strange. Often, a wave of pure, unattached emotion will crash over her—the sickening lurch of terror from the flood, the hollow ache of loss—but with no accompanying image or thought. It is just the feeling, raw and overwhelming. When she does intentionally recall the event, perhaps after hearing the name "Alma" on the news, the memory feels oddly distant, like a story she was told about someone else. She can see the woman in the floodwaters, but it doesn't feel like her. This sense of detachment makes the profound grief that inevitably follows even more confusing. To escape these feelings, Elena has taught herself to "check out." When a trigger is unavoidable, like the sight of a puddle after a downpour, she will fix her gaze on a point on the wall and deliberately try to blank her mind, to leave her body until the worst of it passes. More and more, she finds herself dwelling on the past, scrolling through old photos of her garden, of neighborhood parties, of a life where she did not constantly scan the sky for rain.

It was her daughter’s visit that finally prompted her to seek help. A light drizzle had started, and her daughter found her sitting in the dark, unable to bring herself to turn on a light. The look of deep concern on her daughter’s face made Elena realize that her safe zone had become a cage. She is now terrified that this constant state of threat is her new reality. Her hope for therapy is not grand; it is a simple, desperate wish to feel safe enough to walk in a park again, to hear the rain without her heart beginning to race, and to feel, even for a moment, like the woman she was before the storm.
